# 2 Maccabees Chapter 5 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalence)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 5 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_005_page_001.jpg

---

**1** About this time Antiochus undertook his second campaign against Egypt.

**2** And it came to pass that throughout the city, for almost forty days, there appeared in the air riders on horseback in golden armor, and armed units in full battle array of spears and swords —

**3** companies of cavalry in formation, charges and countercharges on both sides, the brandishing of shields, formations of spears, the flight of arrows, flashing golden ornaments, and armor of every description.

**4** So all men prayed that this apparition would prove to be a good omen.

**5** But a false rumor arose that Antiochus had died. Taking no fewer than a thousand men, Jason made a surprise attack on the city. When the forces on the wall had been pushed back and the city was finally being overrun, Menelaus took refuge in the citadel.

**6** Jason, however, kept slaughtering his own fellow citizens without mercy, not considering that success against one's own kin is the worst kind of failure, but imagining that he was erecting trophies over enemies rather than over fellow countrymen.

**7** Nevertheless, he did not gain control of the government. In the end he received only disgrace from his conspiracy, and went back again as a fugitive to the country of the Ammonites.

**8** Finally he came to a wretched end. Accused before Aretas the ruler of the Arabs, fleeing from city to city, hunted by everyone, hated as a transgressor of the laws and abhorred as the butcher of his country and his compatriots, he was cast ashore in Egypt;

**9** and he who had driven many from their homeland into exile died abroad, having embarked to go to the Lacedaemonians in the hope of finding protection there because of a supposed kinship.

**10** He who had cast out many to lie unburied had no one to mourn for him; he had no funeral of any kind and no burial place in the tombs of his ancestors.

**11** When news of what had occurred reached the king, he concluded that Judea was in revolt. So, raging in spirit, he departed from Egypt and took the city by force of arms.

**12** He ordered his soldiers to cut down without mercy those whom they encountered and to slaughter those who fled into their houses.

**13** There was a massacre of young and old, a destruction of women, children, virgins, and infants.

**14** Within three days, eighty thousand perished — forty thousand killed in hand-to-hand fighting, and as many again sold into slavery.

**15** Not content with this, he had the audacity to enter the most holy temple in all the world, guided by Menelaus, who had turned traitor both to the laws and to his country.

**16** With his defiled hands he seized the sacred vessels, and with his profane hands he swept away what other kings had dedicated for the exaltation, glory, and honor of the place.

**17** Antiochus was swollen with pride, not perceiving that the LORD had been provoked to anger for a short time because of the sins of those who dwelt in the city, and that this was why the place had been left unguarded.

**18** Had it not been that they were already enmeshed in so many sins, this man would have been scourged and turned back from his presumption the moment he advanced, just as Heliodorus had been — he whom King Seleucus sent to inspect the treasury.

**19** But God did not choose the nation for the sake of the holy place; he chose the place for the sake of the nation.

**20** Therefore the holy place itself shared in the calamities that befell the nation and afterward shared in its recovery; what was forsaken in the wrath of the Almighty was restored again in all its glory when the great LORD was reconciled.

**21** So Antiochus, having carried off from the temple eighteen hundred talents, hurried back to Antioch, thinking in his arrogance that he could make the land navigable and the sea passable on foot — so elated was his mind.

**22** He left governors to oppress the people: at Jerusalem, Philip, a Phrygian by birth and in character more barbarous than the man who appointed him;

**23** and at Gerizim, Andronicus; and besides these Menelaus, who treated the citizens more harshly than the others. In his malice toward the Jewish people,

**24** Antiochus dispatched Apollonius, the commander of the Mysians, with an army of twenty-two thousand, commanding him to kill all the grown men and to sell the women and the youth.

**25** When this man arrived in Jerusalem, he made a show of peaceful intentions and waited until the holy sabbath day; then, finding the Jews at rest, he ordered his men to parade in arms.

**26** All those who came out to watch he cut down with the sword; then he rushed into the city with his armed troops and killed great numbers.

**27** But Judas Maccabeus, with about nine others, withdrew into the wilderness and lived in the mountains in the manner of wild animals with his companions, feeding on whatever grew there, so that they might have no share in the defilement.
